paragraphs: Country, and Are So Sensitive in Europe

The temper of the Americans is vindictive, like that of all serious and reflective nations. They hardly ever forget an offense, but it is not easy to offend them, and their resentment is as slow to kindle as it is to fade. In aristocratic communities, where a small number of people manage everything, the outward dealings of men follow settled conventional rules. Everyone then thinks he knows exactly what marks of respect or condescension he should show, and no one is presumed ignorant of the science of etiquette. The usages of the top class in society then serve as a model for all the others. Each of the others also sets up a code of its own, which all its members must follow. Thus the rules of politeness form a complex system of legislation. It is hard to master perfectly, yet dangerous for anyone to depart from, so that men are constantly exposed to giving or receiving bitter affronts without intending to. But as distinctions of rank are wiped out, and men of different education and birth meet and mingle in the same places, it becomes almost impossible to agree on the rules of good breeding. Since its laws are uncertain, breaking them is no crime, even in the eyes of those who know what they are. Men attach more importance to intentions than to forms. They grow less civil, but also less quarrelsome. There are many little attentions an American does not care about. He thinks they are not due to him, or he presumes they are not known to be due. So he either does not notice a rudeness or forgives it. His manners become less courteous, and his character plainer and more manly.

The mutual indulgence of the Americans, and the manly confidence with which they treat each other, also result from another, deeper and more general cause, which I already mentioned in the preceding chapter. In the United States, distinctions of rank in civil society are slight, and in political society they are nonexistent. An American therefore does not think himself bound to pay particular attentions to any of his fellow citizens, nor does he require them from others toward himself. Since he does not see that it is in his interest to seek out the company of any of his countrymen, he is slow to imagine that his own company is being refused. He despises no one because of his station, so he does not imagine anyone can despise him for that reason. Until he has clearly perceived an insult, he does not suppose that an affront was intended. The social condition of the Americans naturally accustoms them not to take offense over small matters. And in turn, the democratic freedom they enjoy spreads this same mildness of temper through the character of the nation. The political institutions of the United States constantly bring citizens of all ranks into contact and force them to pursue great undertakings together. People so engaged have hardly time to attend to the details of etiquette, and they also have too strong an interest in living harmoniously to stick at such things. They soon acquire the habit of paying more attention to the feelings and opinions of those they meet than to their manners, and they do not let trifles annoy them.

I have often noticed in the United States that it is not easy to make a man understand that his presence can be done without. Hints will not always get rid of him. I contradict an American at every word he says, to show him that his conversation bores me, and he instantly sets to work with fresh stubbornness to convince me. I keep a dogged silence, and he thinks I am deep in thought about the truths he is uttering. At last I rush away from his company, and he supposes that some urgent business is calling me elsewhere. This man will never understand that he is wearing me out unless I tell him so, and the only way to be rid of him is to make him my enemy for life.

At first sight it seems surprising that the same man, once transported to Europe, suddenly becomes so touchy and captious that I often find it as hard to avoid offending him here as it was to put him out of countenance there. These two opposite effects come from the same cause. Democratic institutions generally give men a lofty idea of their country and of themselves. An American leaves home with a heart swollen with pride. On arriving in Europe he discovers at once that we are not as absorbed in the United States and the great people who live there as he had supposed, and this begins to annoy him. He has been told that the conditions of society are not equal in our part of the world, and he sees that among the nations of Europe the traces of rank are not wholly erased. Wealth and birth still keep certain vague privileges, which force themselves on his notice while escaping definition. He is therefore profoundly ignorant of the place he ought to occupy in this half-ruined scale of classes, which are distinct enough to hate and despise each other, yet alike enough that he is always confusing them. He is afraid of placing himself too high, and still more afraid of being placed too low. This twofold danger keeps his mind constantly strained and hampers all he says and does. He learns from tradition that in Europe ceremonial observances varied endlessly according to rank. This memory of former times completes his bewilderment, and he fears the more that he will not get the marks of respect due to him, because he does not know exactly what they consist of. He is like a man surrounded by traps. Society is no recreation for him but serious toil. He weighs your least actions, questions your looks, and scrutinizes everything you say, in case some hidden allusion is meant to insult him. I doubt whether there was ever a provincial man of quality so punctilious in his breeding. He tries to observe the slightest rules of etiquette and does not allow one of them to be waived toward himself. He is full of scruples and, at the same time, of pretensions. He wishes to do enough but fears doing too much, and since he does not know very well where the limits of either lie, he keeps up a haughty and awkward air of reserve.

But this is not all; here is yet another duality of the human heart. An American is forever talking about the admirable equality that prevails in the United States. Aloud he makes it his country’s boast, but in secret he laments it for himself, and he aspires to show that he, for his part, is an exception to the general state of things he vaunts. Hardly any American can be found who does not claim some distant kinship with the first founders of the colonies, and as for scions of the noble families of England, America seemed to me to be covered with them. When a wealthy American arrives in Europe, his first concern is to surround himself with all the luxuries of wealth. He is so afraid of being taken for the plain citizen of a democracy that he adopts a hundred contrived ways of putting some new proof of his wealth before you every day. His house will be in the most fashionable part of town, and he will always be surrounded by a crowd of servants. I have heard an American complain that in the best houses of Paris the company was rather mixed. The prevailing taste there was not pure enough for him, and he ventured to hint that, in his opinion, manners there lacked elegance. He could not get used to seeing wit hidden under such unpretending forms.

These contrasts should not surprise us. If the traces of former aristocratic distinctions were not so completely erased in the United States, the Americans would be less simple and less tolerant at home — they would demand less, and be less fond of borrowed manners, in our country.
